newsitem.title: VIETNAM: S.Korea's Kim heads to Vietnam for business drive.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim heads to Vietnam for business drive.

text.p: Intensive preparations were under way in Hanoi on Tuesday for the first ever visit by a South Korean president, who was expected to give a new boost to business ties with Vietnam and put old suspicions to rest.
Huge banners and a welcoming message were draped around the new Hanoi Daewoo Hotel, a joint venture between one of South Korea's biggest companies and a state-owned Vietnamese firm.

Other Korean-Vietnamese ventures took out full-page colour advertisements in the press to greet President Kim Young-sam, and a government-run business magazine ran a special South Korea section headlined: "Kim lends vision with state visit".
"I think my visit will create more momentum for the development of relations between the two countries," Kim told the Vietnam Journalist Association in an interview before his arrival on Wednesday.

Both countries say there are no hard feelings left from the Vietnam War, when South Korea's forces fought alongside the U.S.-backed Saigon administration against North Vietnam. Seoul cut ties with Vietnam when the communist North Vietnamese forces won the war in 1975.
Although diplomatic relations were restored only four years ago, diplomatic, commercial and economic relations have warmed despite the complication of Hanoi's ideological alliance with North Korea.
Diplomats say Seoul considers strong links as crucial, not only because of the communist country's economic revival but also because of regional strategic necessity.
Vietnam is now a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and a prospective member of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
Trade between the two countries totalled $1.54 billion last year, a three-fold increase from 1992, making South Korea Vietnam's third-biggest trading partner.
South Korean firms rank third behind Taiwanese and Singaporean companies in the growing list of countries that have poured investment into Vietnam's booming economy.
Officials said $2.3 billion in direct investment from South Korea had been approved, and predicted that other projects on the drawing board would be given new impetus by Kim's visit.
"It would be advantageous to set up a bridgehead in such a developing nation before anyone else," said Lee Jung-seung, a spokesman for the Daewoo Group, the biggest single investor in Vietnam.

Many South Korean companies feel that way about Vietnam, which they see as a source of cheap and well-educated labour, political stability and an increasingly prosperous population of 75 million people.
Underlining the commercial tilt of his visit, Kim will be accompanied by more than 50 South Korean business executives.
A spokesman for the South Korean Embassy in Hanoi said Kim would sign agreements to set up cooperation studies on nuclear power and the establishment of Vietnam's first stock exchange.
